title: An ode to the humble herring
gist: Reviewing Graeme Rigby's Encyclopaedia of the Herring, Mathew Lyons traces how one fish underwrote Hanseatic Lübeck, supplied 40-50 per cent of Iceland's exports until its 1969 disappearance, and structured Lenten demand across medieval Europe — while stock shifts driven by water temperature were consistently misread as divine judgement, and today's decline is blamed on consumers unwilling to cook.

insights.claim: The Comte de Lacépède wrote in his 1798 Histoire Naturelle des Poissons that the herring is one of those products the use of which decides the destiny of empires.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: The clearest historical statement that a single low-value protein can set the balance of power — the template for arguments about today's chokepoint commodities.
insights.quote: the use of which decides the destiny of empires
insights.locator: The ebb and flow of the herring trade

insights.claim: The Hanse dominated the Baltic herring trade from Lübeck partly because it controlled the supply of salt needed for curing, making control of the complementary input the source of trade dominance.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Own the bottleneck input, not the commodity — the same logic that governs refining, processing and midstream margins today.
insights.quote: It helped that they controlled the supply of salt for curing.
insights.locator: The Hanse dominated the Baltic herring trade

insights.claim: By 1375 the Holy Roman Emperor was calling Lübeck one of the five glories of his dominions and the only one not in Italy, a status built on the herring trade.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Quantifies how far a fishery could lift a northern port into the front rank of European cities.

insights.claim: Charlemagne is said to have founded Hamburg as a herring port in 809, three centuries before Lübeck.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Two of northern Europe's principal commercial cities trace their origin to a single fishery.

insights.claim: At its peak the herring accounted for between 40 and 50 per cent of Iceland's exports, and when the fish disappeared in 1969 quaysides and processing plants were abandoned.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: A textbook single-commodity concentration failure: half of national exports vanishing in one year.

insights.claim: Britain banned all herring fishing for six years around the turn of the 1980s in response to stock collapse.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Total moratorium is the precedent regulators reach for when a fishery fails — the tail scenario for quota-dependent operators.

insights.claim: The Norwegians have a specific word for the phenomenon of herringless waters, calling it a black sea, indicating that stock disappearance was frequent enough to require its own vocabulary.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Recurrence, not novelty: resource collapse in this fishery is a cyclical feature rather than a modern anomaly.

insights.claim: Despite repeated collapses there are still estimated to be a trillion herring in the world's oceans, which the author uses to caution against overstating decline.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: A counterweight to collapse narratives — stock relocation is often mistaken for extinction.
insights.quote: there are still estimated to be a trillion darlings somewhere in the oceans of the world
insights.locator: Let’s not go overboard on such worries

themes.theme: Misreading physical drivers as moral ones

insights.claim: Herring populations move with water temperature and prefer cold water, but to fishermen facing empty nets the shifts looked like caprice, and were read as divine judgement on spilt blood or bad behaviour.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: The archetypal misattribution: a physical supply shift gets explained as moral failure, delaying the correct response.
insights.quote: Science tells us that herring populations adapt to changing water temperatures: they like it cold.
insights.locator: Science tells us that herring populations

insights.claim: William Camden recorded in 1607 that herring which had formerly swarmed only about Norway had by his time moved in great shoals towards English coasts, an early documented relocation of the stock.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Stock migration between national waters is a four-century-old pattern, not a new climate-era phenomenon.
insights.quote: which in the former age swarmed only about Norway, now in our time, by the bounty of divine providence, swim in great shoals towards our coasts
insights.locator: ‘These herrings’, wrote the antiquarian William Camden

insights.claim: In November 1587 two herrings marked with Gothic or Hebrew print were rushed to Frederick II of Norway and Denmark as divine messages; the king was dead within months and the catch continued to decline.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Portent-reading substituted for stock management — the pre-scientific version of narrative-driven decision making.
insights.locator: Other sources tell us that God made his wishes

insights.claim: Before echo-sounding, fishermen located shoals by banging the anchor or rattling chains against the boat and watching for a burst of phosphorescence the Scots called fire in the water.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: A reminder of how recently the search technology that made industrial-scale extraction possible arrived.

insights.claim: The medieval Lenten calendar created structural demand for herring in northern Europe, with the fish embedded in ritual — an effigy of Lent dressed in red and white herring skins at Norwich in 1443, and the Procession of the Herrings at Reims.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Religious observance functioned as a demand mandate; when the mandate goes, the volume goes with it.
insights.locator: Even when abundant, the herring has deep associations with dearth

insights.claim: The Reformation made herring repugnant to the right-thinking sort in England, but by the 16th century England was exporting red herrings to the Ottoman Empire, substituting export markets for lost domestic religious demand.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Export substitution after a domestic demand shock — the standard corporate response to regulatory or cultural demand destruction.
insights.locator: The Reformation may have made herrings repugnant

insights.claim: Nineteenth-century British industrialisation of herring production created a migrant female workforce, the Scottish herring lasses, who followed the season from the Shetlands in May to Great Yarmouth and Lowestoft in November and into the Channel to January.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: A fully mobile seasonal labour force organised around a migrating resource — the physical precursor of modern flexible labour.

insights.claim: Annie Watt's team gutted and packed 288 barrels in four days at Gorleston before the First World War, which the author calculates as 150,000 herring per woman, or 37,500 a shift.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Hard throughput numbers for pre-mechanised processing labour — the productivity baseline that automation had to beat.
insights.quote: that’s 150,000 herring per woman, 37,500 a shift
insights.locator: Rigby cites the example of Annie Watt

insights.claim: Will Buckenham of The Old Smokehouse in Lowestoft, founded in 1760 and the oldest working smokery in Britain, attributes falling sales of red herring, kippers and bloaters to convenience foods and consumers unwilling to cook.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Preparation friction, not taste, is the stated cause of category decline — the same lever that drives packaged-food share gains.
insights.quote: There’s too many… convenience foods and people just don’t want the inconvenience of having to cook.
insights.locator: ‘Sales of red herrin’ and kippers and bloaters

insights.claim: Rigby observes that some twenty-first century cultures have lost a tolerance for strong smelling foods, illustrated by Surströmming from the Gulf of Bothnia, 200 barrels of which once opened together on Ulvön reportedly made birds drop dead from the sky.
insights.speaker: Mathew Lyons
insights.so_what: Sensory tolerance is a moving constraint on which traditional food categories can survive commercially.
